title: What are JavaScript’s primitive types?
answer: JavaScript has seven primitive types: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, symbol, and null. Objects, arrays, and functions are non-primitive. Primitive values are immutable; variables holding them can still be reassigned.
code:
typeof 42; // "number"
typeof null; // "object" (historical quirk)
typeof Symbol(); // "symbol"
tip: Use Array.isArray for arrays; typeof cannot distinguish arrays from other objects.

title: How do null and undefined differ?
answer: undefined often means a value has not been assigned or a property is absent. null is an explicit value commonly used to represent intentional absence. Neither is an object, despite the historical typeof null result.
tip: Default parameters apply for undefined, not for null.

title: What are truthy and falsy values?
answer: Falsy values include false, 0, -0, 0n, an empty string, null, undefined, and NaN. Most other values, including empty arrays and objects, are truthy. Boolean coercion is different from loose equality.
code:
Boolean([]); // true
Boolean({}); // true
Boolean(""); // false
tip: The legacy browser document.all object is also falsy; it is an unusual compatibility exception.

title: How does type coercion work?
answer: JavaScript can convert values implicitly based on an operator. The + operator can concatenate strings, whereas subtraction performs numeric conversion. Prefer explicit conversion at application boundaries to avoid surprising behavior.
tip: Explain the operator and the operand types before predicting the output.

title: What do spread and rest syntax do?
answer: Spread expands an iterable into elements or copies enumerable own properties into an object. Rest collects remaining arguments or properties. Both use three dots, but their role depends on their position. Copies made with spread are shallow.
tip: Object spread does not recursively clone nested objects.

title: How does destructuring work?
answer: Destructuring extracts values from arrays or properties from objects into bindings. You can rename variables and set defaults. A default is used only when the extracted value is undefined.
code:
const { name: displayName, role = "user" } = { name: "Amit" };
const [head, ...tail] = [1, 2, 3];
tip: Destructuring null or undefined as an object throws unless you supply a fallback.

title: Shallow copy vs deep copy: what changes?
answer: A shallow copy creates a new outer container but keeps references to nested objects. A deep copy recursively duplicates supported nested data. structuredClone handles many built-in data types and cycles, but it cannot clone functions or DOM nodes.
tip: JSON serialization is not a universal deep-cloning solution.

title: How do map, filter, and reduce differ?
answer: map transforms each element into a corresponding result. filter retains elements matching a predicate. reduce accumulates elements into one result. They return new results, but your callbacks can still mutate referenced objects if you write them that way.
tip: Use the method that expresses the intended operation, rather than reduce for everything.

title: forEach vs map: which should you choose?
answer: map returns an array of transformed results. forEach returns undefined and is useful for iterating for side effects. Neither method automatically waits for an async callback.
code:
const doubled = [1, 2].map(x => x * 2);
[1, 2].forEach(x => console.log(x));
tip: For sequential awaited work use for...of; for concurrent work await Promise.all(items.map(fn)).

title: How do find, some, and every differ?
answer: find returns the first matching element or undefined. some returns whether at least one element matches; every checks whether all elements match. These methods stop once they can determine the result.
code:
[1, 2, 3].find(x => x > 1); // 2
[1, 2, 3].some(x => x > 2); // true
[].every(x => false); // true
tip: An empty array passes every because there is no counterexample.

title: How do you remove duplicates from an array?
answer: For primitive values, a Set provides uniqueness using SameValueZero comparison. Objects are unique by identity, so two different objects with the same properties remain separate. Deduplicate records by a stable property when that matches your requirements.
tip: A Map keyed by id keeps the last value for duplicate ids.

title: What is the difference between slice and splice?
answer: slice returns a shallow portion of an array without modifying the original. splice removes or inserts items in place and returns removed items. toSpliced is the copying alternative to splice.
tip: Be explicit about mutation when working with React state.

title: How does sort work with numbers?
answer: Array.sort mutates its array and compares string representations by default. Provide a numeric comparator for numbers. toSorted returns a sorted copy. A comparator should be consistent and return negative, zero, or positive values.
tip: Do not write a comparator that only returns true or false.

title: Object vs Map: when should you use each?
answer: Objects are useful for records with named properties. Map is designed for key-value collections, accepts keys of any type, and preserves insertion order. Map also has a direct size property and convenient iteration.
tip: For untrusted keys, Map avoids collisions with inherited object properties.

title: How do optional chaining and nullish coalescing work?
answer: Optional chaining stops property access or a call when its immediate receiver is null or undefined. Nullish coalescing supplies a fallback only for null or undefined, preserving values such as zero or an empty string.
tip: Optional chaining does not protect an undeclared root variable.

title: What is lexical scope?
answer: Lexical scope means accessible bindings are determined by where code is written, rather than where a function is called. Lookup starts in the current environment and proceeds outward. An inner binding can shadow an outer one.
tip: A function does not inherit the local variables of an arbitrary caller.

title: What are call, apply, and bind?
answer: call invokes a function with an explicit this value and separate arguments. apply does the same with an array-like argument list. bind returns a new function with a bound this and optional leading arguments. Arrow functions ignore attempts to rebind their lexical this.
tip: bind does not immediately invoke the target function.

title: What is a higher-order function?
answer: A higher-order function accepts a function as an argument or returns a function. This enables reusable behavior such as mapping, filtering, decorators, and function factories. A callback is the function passed into another function.
tip: Functions are values: they can be stored, passed, and returned.

title: What is currying?
answer: Currying converts a function accepting several arguments into a sequence of functions, typically each taking one argument. It helps specialize reusable operations. Partial application fixes some arguments without necessarily converting the function into unary steps.
tip: Distinguish currying from simply returning any function.

title: What makes a function pure?
answer: A pure function returns the same result for the same inputs and has no externally observable side effects. Reading changing external state or mutating an argument makes reasoning harder. Purity supports predictable tests and React rendering.
code:
const total = prices => prices.reduce((a,b) => a+b, 0);
// No mutation, network calls, or external state.
tip: Logging, DOM changes, and reading the current time are side effects or sources of impurity.

title: How do function declarations and expressions differ?
answer: A function declaration initializes a callable binding when its scope is created. A function expression is evaluated when execution reaches it, and its availability follows the rules of its containing variable. Named expressions also provide a useful local function name.
tip: A const-held function expression is in the temporal dead zone before initialization.

title: What is an IIFE?
answer: An immediately invoked function expression is created and called at once. It can establish a private scope and return a public interface. Modules and block-scoped declarations now cover many of its historical uses.
tip: An IIFE is a pattern, not a separate type of function.

title: What is recursion and what is the base case?
answer: A recursive function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller problem. A base case stops the recursion. Deep recursion can exhaust the JavaScript call stack, so iterative approaches may be safer for large inputs.
tip: Validate the input domain; this simple example assumes a non-negative integer.

title: What happens when you use new?
answer: new creates an object linked to the constructor’s prototype, invokes the constructor with that object as this, and normally returns it. If the constructor explicitly returns an object, that object is returned instead. Arrow functions cannot be used as constructors.
tip: A constructor’s .prototype property differs from the constructor function’s own internal prototype.

title: How do ES modules work?
answer: ES modules use import and export to define dependencies and public bindings. Imports are live read-only views of exported bindings, not copies. Modules run in strict mode. Dynamic import returns a promise and can load modules on demand.
tip: Static import declarations belong at module top level; import() can be called conditionally.

title: Promise.all vs allSettled: what differs?
answer: Promise.all fulfills when every input fulfills and rejects when an input rejects. Promise.allSettled waits for every input to settle and returns status objects. Neither method automatically cancels unfinished operations.
tip: Use all when all results are required; use allSettled when partial outcomes matter.

title: Promise.race vs Promise.any: what differs?
answer: race adopts the first settled outcome, fulfillment or rejection. any fulfills with the first fulfilled outcome and rejects with AggregateError if all inputs reject. Promise.race([]) remains pending; Promise.any([]) rejects.
tip: Losing promises continue running unless you explicitly cancel the underlying operation.

title: How do you handle errors with async/await?
answer: An awaited rejection throws within the async function, where try/catch can handle it. A promise returned without awaiting inside a try block can reject after the block exits. Choose deliberately whether to recover, rethrow, or translate an error.
tip: Do not silently swallow failures that callers need to know about.

title: How can you cancel a fetch request?
answer: Pass an AbortSignal to fetch and call the associated controller’s abort method when the result is no longer needed. Abort also affects response-body reading. Cancellation should be handled separately from real network failures.
tip: In search UIs, also prevent outdated responses from overwriting newer results.

title: Microtasks vs tasks: what runs first?
answer: After the current task finishes and the stack is empty, the browser drains microtasks before moving on to the next task. Promise reactions and queueMicrotask use microtasks; timer callbacks are tasks. Repeatedly adding microtasks can starve other work.
tip: Rendering opportunities are coordinated by the browser; do not promise a paint after every task.

title: What is event capturing vs bubbling?
answer: During capture an event travels through ancestors toward its target. During bubbling it travels back outward for events that bubble. Register capture listeners with the capture option. stopPropagation stops further propagation, but does not cancel a default action.
code:
parent.addEventListener("click", handle, { capture: true });
parent.addEventListener("click", handle); // bubble phase
tip: stopImmediatePropagation also stops later listeners on the current target.

title: preventDefault vs stopPropagation?
answer: preventDefault cancels a cancelable event’s default action, such as submitting a form. stopPropagation stops the event traveling further through the propagation path. They solve different problems; neither implies the other.
tip: A passive event listener cannot prevent the default action.

title: What are common causes of memory leaks?
answer: A leak occurs when data that is no longer useful remains reachable. Common causes include forgotten subscriptions, timers, global collections, and detached DOM nodes still referenced by listeners or closures. Remove references and clean up resources when ownership ends.
tip: Garbage collection is based on reachability, not on whether a variable has left a particular function.

title: What is garbage collection?
answer: JavaScript engines automatically reclaim memory for values that are no longer reachable from roots such as globals and active execution. Algorithms are implementation details. Cycles can be collected if nothing reachable points to the cycle.
code:
let data = { payload: new Array(1000) };
data = null; // Old object may become collectible.
tip: Collection timing is not deterministic, so do not depend on it for resource cleanup.

title: What are WeakMap and WeakSet useful for?
answer: Weak collections do not keep otherwise unreachable keys or members alive. WeakMap is useful for associating private metadata with objects without preventing their collection. These collections are not enumerable and have no size property.
tip: Because garbage-collection timing is hidden, enumeration would expose unstable information.

title: What is a generator function?
answer: A generator function returns an iterator and can pause execution with yield. Calling next resumes execution until the next yield or completion. Generators are useful for lazy sequences and custom iteration; they do not inherently run in parallel.
tip: Async generators combine asynchronous work with iteration through for await...of.

title: What is the iterable protocol?
answer: An iterable provides Symbol.iterator, which returns an iterator. An iterator’s next method returns an object with value and done. for...of, spread, and destructuring consume iterables. Ordinary objects are not iterable by default.
code:
const iterator = [10, 20][Symbol.iterator]();
iterator.next(); // { value: 10, done: false }
tip: for...in enumerates enumerable string property names; it is not a substitute for for...of.

title: What is memoization?
answer: Memoization caches a function’s result for a particular input so repeated calls can reuse work. It is most useful for expensive pure calculations with repeated inputs. A cache also consumes memory and needs an appropriate key and lifetime.
tip: An unbounded cache can become a memory problem.

title: How do you implement a simple debounce?
answer: Keep a timer in a closure. Cancel it whenever a new call arrives, then schedule the latest call. To preserve method context, use a regular wrapper and apply the original this. Production utilities often also expose cancel and flush methods.
tip: A debounce delays execution; it does not cancel a request that has already started.

title: How do you safely update a nested object?
answer: Copy each level on the path you intend to change, keeping unrelated branches shared. Mutating a nested object through a shallow copy still changes the original nested reference. Structural sharing supports efficient identity comparisons.
tip: Copying every object deeply is often unnecessary; copy only the changed paths.

title: What is JSX?
answer: JSX is syntax for describing UI in JavaScript. A build tool transforms it into React element creation calls. It is not HTML: attributes such as className and htmlFor follow React’s conventions, and braces embed JavaScript expressions.
code:
const title =

Hello, {name}

;
tip: JSX expressions describe elements; they do not immediately create DOM nodes.

title: What is a React element vs a component?
answer: A component is a function or other supported component definition that describes how UI is produced. An element is an immutable description of a particular UI node. React uses elements returned by components to determine what to render.
code:
function Welcome() { return

Hello

; } const element = ;
tip: Call components through JSX rather than invoking them as ordinary functions.

title: What is reconciliation?
answer: Reconciliation is how React matches the next UI description with the existing tree. Element types, positions, and keys affect whether identity is preserved or reset. React then commits required host changes, rather than replacing the entire DOM every time.
code: items.map(item => <Row key={item.id} item={item} />);
tip: The virtual DOM is not a guarantee that React is always faster than hand-written DOM code.

title: When does a component re-render?
answer: A component can render when its state updates, its parent renders, or consumed context changes. Memoization can skip some parent-driven renders, but it is an optimization. A render calculates UI; a commit applies actual host changes.
code: setCount(c => c + 1); // schedules a state update
tip: Setting state to an identical value can let React skip updating children.

title: How does React batch state updates?
answer: React can group multiple updates into one render. For a state value calculated from previous state, queue updater functions. Multiple replacements derived from the same render snapshot will not compound in the way multiple updater functions do.
tip: The variable in the current handler still belongs to the current render snapshot.

title: Why must state be treated as immutable?
answer: React expects state to be treated as read-only snapshots. Mutating an existing object can make updates invisible to identity comparisons and also alter previous snapshots. Create a new object or array when updating.
code: setUser(user => ({ ...user, name: "Amit" }));
tip: The setter should receive the new reference; mutating an object and passing it back is unreliable.

title: How do you update an array in React state?
answer: Use copying operations such as map, filter, and spread to add, remove, or replace items. Copy objects inside the array when their properties change. Avoid mutating methods directly on state.
tip: A new array alone does not protect nested objects from mutation.

title: What is lifting state up?
answer: Move shared state to the closest common ancestor of components that need to coordinate. Pass the value down and callbacks up. This establishes a single source of truth instead of synchronizing duplicate state copies.
code: <Temperature value={temperature} onChange={setTemperature} />
tip: Keep state local until another component actually needs to share it.

title: What is prop drilling?
answer: Prop drilling passes data through intermediate components that do not themselves need it. It is not automatically a problem. Composition, moving state closer to consumers, or context can improve a deeply nested data path.
code: <Layout toolbar={<Toolbar user={user} />} />
tip: Try composition before adding a global store for a small UI.

title: What is a custom Hook?
answer: A custom Hook is a function whose name begins with use and which can call other Hooks. It packages reusable stateful logic. Each call gets its own state; sharing a Hook does not share one state instance.
tip: Name ordinary utilities without use if they do not need Hook semantics.

title: How does useRef differ from useState?
answer: useRef returns a stable object with a mutable current property. Changing current does not schedule a render. State is appropriate for data that should change the displayed UI; refs suit DOM handles and values used outside rendering.
tip: Avoid reading or writing mutable refs during render when it makes rendering impure.

title: How do you focus an input in React?
answer: Attach a ref to the input and call its focus method from an event handler or an appropriate effect. Refs provide an escape hatch to imperative browser APIs. Preserve natural keyboard order and avoid unexpected focus jumps.
tip: A ref can be null before mount and after unmount.

title: useEffect vs useLayoutEffect: when to use each?
answer: useLayoutEffect runs after DOM changes but before the browser repaints and can measure or adjust layout. It blocks paint while running. useEffect is usually appropriate for non-layout synchronization and generally allows paint; exact scheduling depends on the interaction.
tip: Prefer useEffect unless you must prevent a visible layout flicker.

title: What does the dependency array control?
answer: React compares effect dependencies with Object.is to decide whether to rerun an effect after a commit. Include every reactive value read by the effect. Omitting the array reruns after every commit; an empty array indicates no reactive dependencies.
tip: An object freshly created on each render has a different identity each time.

title: How do you clean up an effect?
answer: Return a function from the effect to undo subscriptions, timers, or other external synchronization. React runs cleanup before the next setup when dependencies change and on unmount. Cleanup should mirror the setup.
tip: Do not return an async function as the effect itself; its return value would be a promise rather than cleanup.

title: Why does an effect run twice in development?
answer: Strict Mode can run an additional development-only setup and cleanup cycle to expose missing cleanup. It also checks rendering purity. This does not imply production effects always run twice; make setup and cleanup robust rather than hiding the extra call.
tip: Disabling Strict Mode conceals the symptom rather than fixing the resource lifecycle.

title: What is derived state and when should you avoid storing it?
answer: A value calculated from existing props or state often does not need its own state or effect. Calculate it while rendering, and memoize only if the calculation is expensive. Duplicate state creates synchronization bugs and extra renders.
code:
const fullName = firstName + " " + lastName;
const visible = items.filter(item => item.active);
tip: Memoization is a performance choice; avoiding duplicated state is a modeling choice.

title: How does useReducer work?
answer: useReducer models updates as actions handled by a pure reducer. It is useful when state transitions involve related fields or complex rules. dispatch schedules an update; the reducer returns the next state.
tip: Keep side effects out of the reducer.

title: What does React.memo do?
answer: memo can skip rendering a component when its props are unchanged, normally using Object.is for each prop. Its own state and consumed context can still trigger rendering. Fresh function or object props can defeat the optimization.
tip: Profile first; custom comparison functions can cost more than rendering and can introduce stale callbacks.

title: How do you avoid unnecessary renders?
answer: Start by locating the measured cost. Keep state near its consumers, avoid unnecessary effects, and keep component boundaries sensible. Memoize expensive calculations or components only when identity stability and profiling support it.
code: const filtered = useMemo(() => expensiveFilter(items), [items]);
tip: A render is not automatically slow and does not necessarily change the DOM.

title: What is code splitting with lazy and Suspense?
answer: lazy defers loading a component module until it is needed. Suspense provides a fallback while a descendant suspends. Declare lazy components outside other components to preserve identity. Loading failures should be handled with an error boundary.
code:
const Editor = lazy(() => import("./Editor")); Loading editor…

}>
tip: The imported module normally needs a default component export.

title: What is an error boundary?
answer: An error boundary catches rendering and lifecycle errors in its descendant component tree and shows fallback UI. It does not generally catch event-handler errors or arbitrary asynchronous callbacks. Class components can implement it; libraries provide convenient wrappers.
code:
Something went wrong.

}>
tip: Handle event-handler failures with normal try/catch or promise handling.

title: What are portals?
answer: A portal renders children into a different DOM container while keeping them in the same React tree. Context and React event propagation follow the React tree. Portals are useful for overlays, but accessibility and focus management remain your responsibility.
code:
createPortal(
Dialog content
, document.body);
tip: A portal alone does not trap focus or make a dialog accessible.

title: What are fragments used for?
answer: A fragment groups children without adding a wrapper DOM element. The short syntax is <>...</>. When mapping groups that need keys, use the explicit Fragment component with a key.
tip: Short fragment syntax cannot receive a key.

title: How do you conditionally render content?
answer: Use normal JavaScript conditions, ternaries, and logical operators to choose React content. Return null to render nothing. Be careful with numeric expressions on the left of &&, because zero is rendered as text.
code:
{items.length > 0 && <List items={items} />}
{loading ? <Spinner /> : <Profile />}
tip: Do not conditionally call Hooks while choosing what content to return.

title: How do React event handlers work?
answer: Pass a function to an event prop such as onClick. React invokes it for the interaction. Calling a function while assigning the prop executes it during rendering instead. Event handlers are a suitable place for user-triggered side effects.
code:
<button onClick={() => save(id)}>Save</button>
// Avoid onClick={save(id)} unless save intentionally returns a handler.
tip: The callback must not mutate props or state directly.

title: How do you prevent a form reload in React?
answer: Handle the form’s onSubmit event and call preventDefault when JavaScript should manage submission. Read inputs with controlled state or FormData. Keep native labels, input types, and validation where they fit.
tip: Handle onSubmit on the form so keyboard submission works too.

title: What is hydration?
answer: Hydration attaches React behavior to HTML produced on the server or at build time. The initial client render should match that HTML. Browser-only values, random values, or inconsistent markup can cause mismatches.
tip: Effects run on the client; hiding a warning does not fix a mismatched initial UI.

title: Server Components vs Client Components?
answer: Server Components execute in a server or build environment and can access server-side resources without shipping their component code to the browser. Client Components support state, effects, and interactions. The use client directive establishes a client module boundary.
tip: A Client Component can still have its initial HTML prerendered; client does not always mean no server HTML.

title: What is useTransition used for?
answer: useTransition marks eligible state updates as non-urgent so React can keep urgent interactions responsive. The pending state lets you communicate work in progress. Controlled text-input updates must remain urgent.
code:
const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();
startTransition(() => setTab("results"));
tip: A transition does not make an expensive JavaScript calculation itself run on a worker.

title: What is useDeferredValue used for?
answer: useDeferredValue lets a part of the UI lag behind an urgent value while React works on a background render. It can improve responsiveness when an expensive view depends on typing. It is not a fixed-delay debounce and does not prevent network requests by itself.
code:
const deferredQuery = useDeferredValue(query);
<ExpensiveResults query={deferredQuery} />
tip: Memoizing the expensive child can help it skip urgent renders with unchanged deferred props.

title: How do you reset a component’s state?
answer: State is associated with a component’s identity in the tree. Changing its key or type recreates the component and resets its state. Use this deliberately for a new form entity; unstable keys cause unintended resets.
code: <ProfileForm key={userId} userId={userId} />
tip: Do not define component functions inside a parent render when you need their identity preserved.

title: Why is using array indexes as keys risky?
answer: When list order changes, an index key identifies the position rather than the underlying item. Stateful rows can then keep state that belonged to a different item. Stable data ids preserve the intended association across insertion, deletion, and reordering.
code: rows.map(row => <EditableRow key={row.id} row={row} />);
tip: Index keys can be acceptable for truly static lists with no identity-sensitive changes.

title: How can fetch effects avoid race conditions?
answer: A slower earlier request can finish after a newer request and overwrite the UI. Use cleanup to abort supported requests and/or ignore results from obsolete effect instances. Also handle errors and loading state deliberately.
tip: Framework data-fetching tools can handle caching and request coordination more comprehensively.

title: What is a stale state update in an async handler?
answer: An async handler retains the render snapshot in which it started. After await, closed-over values do not automatically become current. Use updater functions when calculating next state from previous state, and model request identity when ordering matters.
code:
await save();
setCount(c => c + 1);
tip: A functional updater fixes dependent increments; it does not solve every stale-data race.

title: What is useId for?
answer: useId generates an id suitable for associating accessibility attributes such as a label and input. It supports server/client consistency when used correctly. It is not intended for list keys; those should come from the data.
tip: Do not call useId inside a loop to generate list keys.

title: What is useImperativeHandle?
answer: useImperativeHandle customizes the handle exposed through a ref, allowing a child to offer a small imperative API such as focus. Prefer declarative props when possible. In React 19 function components can receive ref as a prop.
tip: Older React versions commonly use forwardRef to receive the ref.

title: How do you choose between Context and a state library?
answer: Context transports values through a subtree; it is not a complete data architecture. A state library may add selectors, external subscriptions, tooling, or coordinated updates. Choose based on update frequency, ownership, and measured rendering needs.
code:
const theme = useContext(ThemeContext);
// A theme is a natural context use case.
tip: Do not move every local form field into globally shared state.

title: What should you test in a React component?
answer: Test observable behavior: what users see, type, click, and receive as feedback. Cover important success, failure, loading, and keyboard paths. Tests that only duplicate implementation details are brittle when refactoring.
code:
// Example behavior:
// Type a name → submit → see a success message.
tip: Prefer accessible queries such as role and label when using a component testing library.

title: How do you make an accessible React UI?
answer: Use semantic HTML, visible labels, keyboard-accessible controls, and appropriate focus management. Announce important dynamic status changes with live regions where appropriate. React does not make inaccessible markup accessible automatically.
code: {message}
tip: Custom interactive widgets need the same behaviors users expect from native controls.

title: What does the doctype do?
answer: The HTML doctype triggers standards mode in modern browsers. Without an appropriate doctype, a browser may use quirks mode and emulate legacy layout behavior. The doctype is a declaration, not an HTML element.
code:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">…</html>
tip: Check document.compatMode when diagnosing unexpected quirks behavior.

title: What belongs in head vs body?
answer: head contains document metadata and references such as title, meta, styles, and scripts. body contains the document’s main rendered content. Scripts can appear in either place, but loading strategy affects parsing and execution.
code: Learn HTML
tip: Document metadata is different from visible page headings.

title: Why should you set the document language?
answer: The lang attribute identifies the content’s language. Assistive technology uses it for pronunciation, and other tools can use it for language handling. Mark a language change on a nested element when a passage uses another language.
code: नमस्ते
tip: Language identification supports accessibility but does not translate content.

title: What is the purpose of meta charset?
answer: The charset declaration tells the browser how to decode the document’s bytes. UTF-8 supports characters from many writing systems. Put the declaration early in the document, within the first 1024 bytes.
code: <meta charset="utf-8">
tip: Correct encoding matters before the browser can interpret the document’s text.

title: How do id and class differ?
answer: An id should uniquely identify an element within its document and can be a fragment target or accessibility reference. A class is a reusable token for grouping elements. CSS and DOM APIs can select both.

tip: Duplicate ids can break labels, fragment navigation, and script lookups.

title: What are global attributes?
answer: Global attributes can be used on all HTML elements, although their effect depends on the element and context. Examples include id, class, lang, hidden, title, and data-* attributes. An attribute’s presence is not proof that it is appropriate for every purpose.
code: <section id="intro" class="chapter" lang="en">…</section>
tip: title is not a reliable replacement for visible labels or accessible naming.

title: How do boolean attributes work?
answer: For HTML boolean attributes, presence generally means true and absence means false. Writing disabled="false" still disables a control because the attribute is present. ARIA attributes have different value rules.
code:
<button disabled>Unavailable</button>
<!-- disabled="false" is still disabled -->
tip: In React, pass disabled={false} to omit the boolean attribute.

title: What is the difference between strong and b?
answer: strong marks content with strong importance, seriousness, or urgency. b draws attention without adding that importance, such as a keyword in a summary. Their default bold appearance can be changed with CSS.
code: Warning: This action deletes the draft.
tip: Choose semantics based on meaning, not on default font weight.

title: What is the difference between em and i?
answer: em indicates stress emphasis that can change the meaning of a sentence. i marks text in an alternate voice or convention, such as a technical term. Both are often italic by default, but visual styling is not their meaning.
code: I did send it. The term closure has a specific meaning.
tip: Use CSS for purely visual italics when no semantic distinction is intended.

title: section vs article vs div: which fits?
answer: article represents a self-contained composition that could stand independently. section groups a thematic part of a document, usually with a heading. div is a generic container when no more meaningful element fits.

tip: Do not replace every div with section without considering document structure.

title: How should you structure headings?
answer: Use heading levels to express content hierarchy, rather than choosing them for font size. A clear main heading and logically nested subheadings support navigation and comprehension. Apply visual appearance with CSS independently.
code:

tip: A heading should describe the section that follows it.

title: What are landmark elements?
answer: Elements such as main, nav, header, footer, and aside can expose meaningful landmarks to assistive technology, depending on context. They help users navigate to major parts of the page. Label multiple navigation landmarks when their purposes differ.
code:
<nav aria-label="Primary">…</nav>
<main id="main">…</main>
<nav aria-label="Footer">…</nav>
tip: Use one visible main landmark for the page’s primary content.

title: When should you use ARIA?
answer: Use ARIA when native semantics cannot express the required accessible meaning. ARIA changes the accessibility representation, not keyboard behavior or appearance. Prefer native HTML controls, and avoid roles that conflict with actual behavior.
code: <button aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="details">Details</button>
tip: No ARIA is often better than incorrect ARIA.

title: What is an accessible name?
answer: An accessible name is the label assistive technology uses to identify a control or element. It can come from visible text, an associated label, aria-labelledby, or aria-label according to the naming rules. Prefer a visible label that everyone can understand.
code: <button aria-label="Close question">×</button>
tip: An icon alone often does not communicate a meaningful accessible name.

title: How does tabindex affect keyboard navigation?
answer: tabindex="0" includes an element in the normal tab order. tabindex="-1" allows programmatic focus without adding a tab stop. Positive values create a custom order and are usually best avoided. Native controls already have appropriate focus behavior.
code: <main id="main" tabindex="-1">…</main>
tip: Adding tabindex to a div does not give it button keyboard behavior.

title: What is a skip link?
answer: A skip link lets keyboard users jump past repeated navigation to the main content. It can become visible on focus and point to the main region. Ensure the target can receive focus appropriately.
code:
Skip to content
…
tip: Do not hide the link in a way that also prevents keyboard access.

title: How do aria-live regions work?
answer: A live region asks assistive technology to announce changes to its content. role="status" provides a polite status announcement. Reserve assertive announcements for urgent information so ordinary updates do not interrupt users excessively.
code: Saved successfully.
tip: A live region is not a replacement for good focus management.

title: What does inert do?
answer: The inert attribute makes an element’s subtree unavailable for interaction and normally removes it from the accessibility tree. It can keep background content inactive while a custom overlay is open. Visual styling and focus placement still need consideration.
code: Background content
tip: A modal dialog also needs a clear accessible name and a way to close it.

title: How does the dialog element work?
answer: dialog is a native container for dialogs. Calling showModal displays it modally, makes the rest of the document inert, and places it in the top layer. Calling show creates a non-modal dialog. Provide a label and sensible initial focus.
code: Confirm
tip: Using the open attribute alone does not create the same modal behavior as showModal.

title: How do details and summary work?
answer: details creates a native disclosure widget. Its first summary provides the interactive label, and the remaining content is expanded or collapsed. The open attribute controls its expanded state. This is a useful alternative to custom accordion JavaScript.
code:
What is a closure?

A function with access to its lexical environment.
tip: Keep the summary text meaningful when read without the expanded content.

title: What do action and method do on a form?
answer: action specifies the submission destination. method controls how form data is submitted, commonly GET or POST. GET places data in the URL; POST usually sends it in the request body. HTTPS is needed for transport protection either way.
code:
<form action="/search" method="get">
  <input name="q"><button>Search</button>
</form>
tip: POST alone does not encrypt data or provide CSRF protection.

title: Why does an input need a name?
answer: The name attribute identifies a successful control’s value in native form submission and FormData. id associates labels and selects an element; it does not replace name. Disabled controls are generally omitted from submitted data.
code: <input id="email" name="email" type="email">
tip: An unchecked checkbox is normally omitted rather than sent as false.

title: disabled vs readonly: what differs?
answer: Disabled controls are generally not focusable or submitted and do not participate in constraint validation. Readonly controls of supported types remain focusable and submit their values, but the user cannot edit them. readonly does not apply to every control type.
code:
<input name="id" value="123" readonly>
<input name="hiddenFromSubmit" value="x" disabled>
tip: Neither attribute should be trusted as server-side authorization.

title: What is native constraint validation?
answer: Input types and attributes such as required, min, max, pattern, and minlength define constraints checked by the browser. checkValidity returns a boolean and reportValidity can show feedback. Client validation improves UX but must be repeated on the server.
code:
<input type="email" required>
<input type="number" min="18" max="100">
tip: A valid email syntax does not prove that the address exists.

title: How do radio buttons and checkboxes differ?
answer: Radio buttons sharing a name form a group where one option can be selected. Checkboxes represent independent on/off choices. Use fieldset and legend to label a related group. Explicit value attributes define the submitted option.
code:
<fieldset><legend>Theme</legend>
<label><input type="radio" name="theme" value="light">Light</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="theme" value="dark">Dark</label>
</fieldset>
tip: Every individual control still needs its own label.

title: What does autocomplete do?
answer: autocomplete tells the browser what a field represents so it can offer suitable stored values. Use standard tokens such as name, email, current-password, and new-password. Browsers may apply their own policies even when autocomplete is off.
code: <input name="email" type="email" autocomplete="email">
tip: Correct tokens improve both usability and accessibility.

title: How do GET and POST form submissions differ?
answer: GET encodes fields into a query string and suits retrieval that can be bookmarked. POST submits data in a body and suits operations that change server state. Neither method alone supplies encryption or reliable security checks.
code: <form action="/profile" method="post">…</form>
tip: Do not put sensitive form values in a GET query string.

title: How do you associate error text with an input?
answer: Provide specific error text and reference it with aria-describedby. Set aria-invalid when the input is invalid. Explain how to correct the problem, and ensure submission errors can be found without relying on color alone.
code: Enter a valid email address.
tip: Do not mark an untouched optional field invalid without a reason.

title: What should alt text contain?
answer: Alt text communicates an image’s purpose in its context. Meaningful images need useful alternatives; purely decorative images usually need alt="". Complex diagrams may also need an adjacent full explanation. Do not repeat nearby text unnecessarily.
tip: A file name or the phrase image of is rarely a useful alternative by itself.

title: picture vs img: when should you use each?
answer: img displays an image and provides the alt text. picture wraps sources to choose alternate crops or formats while retaining a required img fallback. Use srcset and sizes on img for resolution switching when the composition stays the same.
tip: picture is not automatically more performant; provide the resources that match your layout.

title: What do loading and decoding do on images?
answer: loading="lazy" lets the browser defer offscreen images. decoding="async" is a hint that image decoding may happen asynchronously. These are browser hints, not exact scheduling guarantees. Reserve space with dimensions to avoid layout shifts.
tip: Avoid lazy-loading the main image needed for the initial visible screen.

title: How do you create an accessible data table?
answer: Use table for tabular relationships, with caption for its title and th elements for headers. scope="col" or scope="row" associates simple headers with cells. Complex tables may require explicit headers relationships. Tables are not page-layout tools.
code:
Scores
NameScore
Amit92
tip: Keep relationships understandable when the table is read in a linear order.

title: What is an iframe and how do you use it safely?
answer: iframe embeds another browsing context. Provide a descriptive title and restrict powerful features where possible. sandbox can apply restrictions, while allow controls selected permissions. Embedded untrusted content needs careful origin and capability boundaries.
code: <iframe src="/preview" title="Code preview" sandbox></iframe>
tip: Combining allow-scripts and allow-same-origin for same-origin content can undermine sandboxing.

title: How do audio and video elements work?
answer: Native audio and video elements provide playback for media sources. controls exposes browser controls. Add captions through track for video and offer appropriate transcripts. Autoplay may be blocked and should not be assumed to work.
code:
<video controls>
  <source src="lesson.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  <track kind="captions" src="captions.vtt" srclang="en" label="English">
</video>
tip: Captions need timing and meaningful text, not just an empty track tag.

title: How do SVG and canvas differ?
answer: SVG describes vector shapes as DOM elements and scales cleanly. Canvas provides a bitmap drawing surface controlled through drawing commands. SVG suits interactive diagrams; canvas suits large numbers of frequently redrawn objects. Both require accessible alternatives where needed.
code:
<svg viewBox="0 0 100 100" role="img" aria-label="Blue circle">
  <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="30" fill="blue"/>
</svg>
tip: Canvas pixels do not automatically expose individual drawn objects to assistive technology.

title: What is a template element?
answer: template stores an inert HTML fragment that is not rendered until instantiated. JavaScript can clone its content and insert it into the document. This is useful for reusable markup without constructing HTML strings.
code:
const clone = template.content.cloneNode(true);
document.querySelector("main").append(clone);
tip: Cloning copies structure, not listeners added with addEventListener to the original nodes.

title: What is the difference between hidden and aria-hidden?
answer: hidden normally prevents content from being rendered and exposed to assistive technology. aria-hidden removes content from the accessibility tree but does not visually hide it or disable focus. Avoid hiding focusable interactive content only from assistive technology.

tip: Use aria-hidden for redundant decorative content, not as a substitute for hiding an inactive UI.

title: How do preload, prefetch, and preconnect differ?
answer: preload asks the browser to fetch a resource needed for the current navigation. prefetch hints at a resource likely useful later. preconnect warms a connection to an origin. Hints consume resources, so add them only for a concrete loading need.
code: <link rel="preload" href="/font.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>
tip: Incorrect preload attributes can cause duplicate downloads instead of a speedup.

title: What is contenteditable?
answer: contenteditable makes an element’s content editable in the browser. It does not provide a complete rich text editor or safe serialization by itself. Handle pasted content, keyboard behavior, focus, and storage carefully.
code: Edit this text
tip: Treat user-authored markup as untrusted; avoid injecting it back with unsanitized innerHTML.

title: How do you open links in a new tab safely?
answer: target="_blank" asks for a new browsing context. Modern browsers generally apply noopener behavior implicitly, but explicit rel="noopener" documents the intention. noreferrer also suppresses the Referer header and implies noopener.
code: Documentation
tip: Warn users about unexpected new-tab behavior when the context makes it confusing.
